title: Regional surge mitigation and fallback runbook workshop
summary: Technical deep-dive workshop to define policy routing and surge mitigation runbook for Apricot Labs' multi-region serving. Covered thresholds for regional capacity, KV cache priming, fallback sequencing, health checks, and rollback criteria. Agreed on benchmarks and a staged pilot across three regions.
next_steps: SE to run synthetic surge benchmark across three regions and share spreadsheet (Ethan)
AE to send draft runbook and pricing implications
Customer to provide traffic pattern samples and list of compliance constraints
Schedule pilot kickoff for week of 2025-10-20
action_items: Ethan Park: run 3-region KV cache + batching surge benchmark and upload results to shared spreadsheet by 2025-10-16
Maya Chen: send DR runbook draft + pricing delta for dedicated capacity by 2025-10-12
Priya Sharma: provide 7-day hourly traffic sample and list of critical endpoints by 2025-10-13
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-10-09 15:00 PT
Duration: 72 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Priya Sharma (Apricot Labs - Platform Eng), Liam O'Connor (Apricot Labs - SRE), Sarah Y. (Apricot Labs - CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough): align on runbook -- define thresholds -- KV cache warmup -- route down to fallback model/region -- smoke tests and rollback

[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call? (laughs) we got like 72 minutes, so we'll try to be pragmatic.
[00:00:12] Priya Sharma: hey Maya, Priya here. Liam and Sarah are on as well.
[00:00:16] Liam O'Connor: Liam here. ok.
[00:00:18] Sarah Y.: Sarah here.
[00:00:22] Maya Chen: Cool. Ethan, wanna kick off on the problem statement? what are we seeing in staging and what are the pain points.
[00:00:30] Ethan Park: sure. so Apricot's main issue is sudden regional surges — you know, traffic spikes in eu-west that blow out your TPU/GPU pool and then requests either queue up or fail over to the US which increases latencies and costs. we've looked at a couple things: policy-based routing, prefilling KV caches in secondary regions, and using a lightweight quantized fallback model for SLO preservation.
[00:00:58] Priya Sharma: yep, that's accurate. we saw two 10x spikes last month during product launches. the problem was KV cache misses in the failover region and a cold cache causing 400–800ms extra tail latency.
[00:01:18] Ethan Park: exactly. and the KV cache behavior is important — it's not just key presence, it's prefix cache and the way we warm the kv by replaying hot prefixes or using replicated snapshots.
[00:01:34] Maya Chen: quick question — are we talking active-active or active-passive for Apricot's setup? Priya?
[00:01:40] Priya Sharma: we currently run active-active for read traffic but write auth/state is centralized. we want active-active for inference ideally, but budget constraints mean we might do active-primary with warm standby regions.
[00:01:54] Ethan Park: ok, that maps to two patterns. runbook will need different steps for active-active (auto-shard routing) vs primary-standby (fast failover + cache priming). we'll propose both.

[00:02:16] Liam O'Connor: can we talk about thresholds? like at what CPU/GPU utilization do we trigger a reroute? we need concrete numbers.
[00:02:23] Ethan Park: recommended starting point: soft threshold at 70% GPU util sustained for 30s, hard threshold at 85% sustained for 15s. soft threshold starts a progressive reroute for low-latency customers, hard threshold triggers global fallback policy.
[00:02:43] Priya Sharma: 70% seems low but i get the progressive reroute idea, we do want to protect tail latency.
[00:02:49] Ethan Park: also we can use queue depth and 95/99p latency as signals, not just util. e.g., if queue depth > 100 for > 60s or 99p > 600ms then escalate.

[00:03:10] Maya Chen: let's write that down as the first block in the runbook: metrics to watch.

[00:03:22] Ethan Park: on KV cache, two strategies: proactive snapshot replication at configured intervals (say every 10 minutes for hot prefixes), or on-demand prime by replaying last N requests for heavy keys. snapshot replication costs network and storage but gives immediate warm cache; replay is cheaper but slower.
[00:03:44] Priya Sharma: replay might be fine. we have a durable event log that can replay, but time to prime is like 20–30s for the top 1k prefixes.
[00:03:56] Ethan Park: okay so for runbook we recommend: for warm standby regions, run snapshot every 5–15 minutes for top-tier caches; have high-priority prime path for top 200 prefixes on hard failover.

[00:04:12] Sarah Y.: what about consistency — if we replicate snapshots there is a chance of serving slightly stale cache content, which is acceptable for inference, right?
[00:04:20] Maya Chen: typically acceptable, esp for product recommender style features. we should document staleness windows and include a canary flag for any stateful outputs.

[00:04:33] Liam O'Connor: batching — how does Redwood handle dynamic batching across regions? if we switch routing, does batch efficiency drop?
[00:04:41] Ethan Park: batching is workload-aware. moving a subset of traffic reduces batch sizes until we reach a new steady state. in practice you see small latency bumps for 30–90s as batching warms. the runbook should include a staged reroute to avoid batch collapse — e.g., move 10% of low-priority traffic every 15s.

[00:05:02] Priya Sharma: so progressive reroute + batch-aware stepdowns. noted.

[00:05:12] Maya Chen: model fallbacks — we discussed using a quantized variant for hotspots. Ethan, can you describe the tradeoffs?
[00:05:18] Ethan Park: sure. quantized models (4-bit/8-bit) give 2–4x throughput and lower memory but may introduce small quality regressions. for critical SLAs we prefer a two-tier approach: try the same model variant first (scale up), if that fails, route to quantized small model, then as last resort route to a cheaper generative proxy or cached response.
[00:05:40] Liam O'Connor: do we have metrics for perceptible quality loss? our product team will want A/B evals.
[00:05:45] Ethan Park: we typically run nll/embedding-sim tests and a small eval set to catch regressions. will run a quick A/B during pilot.

[00:05:58] Maya Chen: good. let's also define health checks and smoke tests for any failover event.
[00:06:03] Ethan Park: recommended smoke tests: synthetic token generation at 1 qps to main endpoint, a 5qps steady-state check, and a KV read check returning expected prefixes. if smoke tests fail we rollback routing within X minutes.

[00:06:18] Priya Sharma: rollback criteria? like if latency degrades beyond baseline by 20% or errors increase 2x, we roll back.
[00:06:26] Ethan Park: yes — baseline comparison windows should be configurable; recommend 5-minute rolling window.

[00:06:34] Maya Chen: I want to be explicit: rollback cadence and who executes it. Priya, do you want your SREs to have runbook permissions or should Redwood execute failover remotely?
[00:06:44] Priya Sharma: we'd prefer to keep control internally, but Redwood can provide an optional managed failover for emergencies with a signed playbook.
[00:06:54] Maya Chen: perfect.

[00:07:05] Liam O'Connor: VPC/on-prem questions — if we do private deployment, how different is the runbook? do you still handle KV snapshot replication? network egress?
[00:07:15] Ethan Park: for private deployments in customer VPC, KV replication can be either via s3-compatible snapshot push or via dedicated peering. network costs and permissions are handled by customer's infra. Redwood's control plane can orchestrate but data plane is in VPC; so the runbook will include steps to trigger snapshot pushes and monitor s3 object timestamps.
[00:07:39] Priya Sharma: we probably want snapshots to be pulled (not pushed) from our side for security reasons.
[00:07:45] Ethan Park: that's fine — we'll add pull mode to the runbook and an auth checklist.

[00:07:52] Maya Chen: let's talk about measurement and benchmarks we'll run in pilot.
[00:07:57] Ethan Park: pilot tests: 1) cold-start failover: create an induced outage in primary region and measure 99/95p latency in standby for the first 10 minutes; 2) surge replay: replay realistic traffic trace scaled by 5x against multi-region setup to test progressive reroute; 3) KV cache warmup timing for top prefixes; 4) quantized fallback accuracy vs baseline.
[00:08:26] Priya Sharma: can you include a spreadsheet template for recording results?
[00:08:30] Maya Chen: yes, Ethan will share. we'll link in the runbook.

[00:08:36] Ethan Park: quick note on routing policies: we support weighted traffic shifts, priority-based rules per tenant, and SLO-driven automated shifts. the SLO-driven rules need a policy that maps signals to actions (e.g., signal: 99p latency > 600ms -> action: move 20% of traffic away from region per 30s until stabilizes).
[00:09:02] Sarah Y.: important for us: per-tenant priority. some customers are high-value and can't accept degradation, we need sticky routing for them.
[00:09:10] Maya Chen: yep, we can pin high-value tenants to dedicated capacity or exempt them from progressive shifting.

[00:09:22] Liam O'Connor: what about throttles and backpressure signaling — can Redwood bubble back signals to clients so we can degrade gracefully?
[00:09:30] Ethan Park: we have token-level throttles and headers that indicate degraded mode. you could read 'X-Redwood-Mode: degraded' and serve a local fallback on your side.

[00:09:42] Priya Sharma: security and compliance — audit logs, KMS key rotation, and SOC 2. we need logs for any routing event.
[00:09:50] Maya Chen: runbook will include an 'audit trail' section with required fields: event id, timestamp, initiator, policy trigger, actions taken, artifacts (snapshots pushed), and link to benchmark results. Redwood keeps those in console and can forward an export to your SIEM.

[00:10:10] Ethan Park: another operational detail: when snapshot replication is used, include a checksum step and optional integrity check to avoid serving corrupted caches.

[00:10:22] Maya Chen: good call. ok let's do a quick walkthrough of an example scenario — we'll roleplay a region efflux event.

[00:10:30] Ethan Park: scenario: eu-west primary hits 90% GPU util and queue depth spike. Step 1: soft alerts at 70% for 30s. Step 2: begin progressive reroute of non-gated traffic 10% per 15s. Step 3: initiate KV snapshot prime for top 200 prefixes to standby. Step 4: if 85% sustained for 15s or 99p > 800ms -> escalate to hard fallback: shift 50% traffic and bring up quantized model pool. Step 5: run smoke tests and validate.
[00:11:05] Priya Sharma: in that scenario, who flips the routing? we will, but i'd like Redwood to provide a trigger endpoint for quick ops.
[00:11:13] Maya Chen: can do — we'll include an authenticated playbook endpoint and an ops runbook for calling it.

[00:11:20] Liam O'Connor: what's the expected warmup time for the quantized pool?
[00:11:24] Ethan Park: for a cold quantized pool on GPU nodes, ~20–50s to provision and load weights, but we can pre-warm a tiny fleet if needed which keeps cost low but reduces provisioning to <10s.

[00:11:41] Sarah Y.: cost delta — how much more expensive if we keep warm standby vs cold on-demand?
[00:11:46] Maya Chen: we put numbers in the pricing doc but rough ballpark: warm standby with small fraction of capacity (10% region capacity) costs ~20–30% of full active cost, whereas cold on-demand is near zero until spin-up but has latency risk.

[00:12:02] Ethan Park: billing nuance: we can meter warm standby differently — reserve a minimal footprint and bill at reduced rate; dedicated commitments can get discounts.

[00:12:12] Priya Sharma: ok that's fine. next let's outline acceptance criteria for pilot.
[00:12:18] Maya Chen: acceptance: 1) failover 99p within 2x baseline for 5 minutes in induced outage; 2) KV cache warmup for 95% of hot prefixes within 60s; 3) no more than 1% error increase during progressive reroutes; 4) runbook and audit logs available.

[00:12:40] Ethan Park: we'll capture those in the spreadsheet template.

[00:12:46] Maya Chen: any other questions from Apricot team?
[00:12:50] Priya Sharma: one more — can Redwood help with runbook drills? weekly dry runs?
[00:12:55] Ethan Park: yes, we can schedule tabletop drills and simulate outages in a non-prod environment.

[00:13:03] Liam O'Connor: can we add an appendix about edge cache eviction policies? our working set changes fast.
[00:13:09] Ethan Park: yes, eviction TTLs and LFU/LRU knobs will be in appendix. also add cache partitioning suggestions for multi-tenant workloads.

[00:13:20] Maya Chen: ok big picture — we'll send draft runbook, Ethan will run benchmarks, Apricot provides traces, and we'll reconvene next week to review results.

[01:11:58] Maya Chen: quick recap:
- thresholds and signals defined
- KV snapshot vs replay strategies
- progressive reroute and batching considerations
- quantized fallback and warm pool options
- smoke tests and rollback metrics
- pilot acceptance criteria

[01:12:10] Priya Sharma: thanks everyone. looking forward to the doc. we'll aim to have the traffic samples by monday.

End transcript
